passage:
"Preeti! You picked up!"
"Zubin, it's been three months. Of course I picked up."
"I'm sorry. The job's been crazy. I kept meaning to call."
"I know. Me too, with the thesis." She paused. "Honestly, I thought we were drifting."
"We are. That's why I'm calling." He took a breath. "What if we set a thing? Every second Sunday, a call. Even ten minutes."
"That sounds like a meeting."
"A meeting with chai and gossip."
She laughed. "Okay. And if one of us cancels?"
"Then that person sends a voice note with a full update. Punishment."
"Deal."
"And when I come to Pune in May—"
"You're staying at mine. No hotel."
"Deal."

qa.q: How often did Zubin suggest they call?
qa.a: He suggested every second Sunday.

qa.q: What was Preeti feeling before Zubin's call?
qa.a: She was worried they were drifting apart and perhaps a little hurt by the three months of silence.

qa.q: Why is a regular call a good idea for keeping their friendship alive?
qa.a: A fixed small commitment, even ten minutes, makes staying in touch easier than waiting for free time that never comes.

qa.q: How might Zubin feel after the call?
qa.a: He probably feels relieved and happy that Preeti still wants to stay close, and reassured by her offer to host him.

grounding: It shows two young friends making a practical plan to keep their friendship alive despite distance and busy schedules.

passage: When I left for my first job in Hyderabad, I thought my school friendships would last forever on their own. I'm Samir. Disha and I had been best friends since Class 6. For the first year we texted every day. By the second, it was once a month. Then she got engaged, and I found out from a photo online. That stung. I realised I'd stopped asking about her life. I'd send memes, not questions. So I called her, apologised, and asked about the wedding. We talked for two hours. Now we have a shared playlist and add songs every week, and I actually put her birthday in my calendar. I flew back for her wedding. It's not the same as school, but it's real.

qa.q: How did Samir find out Disha got engaged?
qa.a: Samir found out from a photo online.

qa.q: Why did finding out from a photo sting Samir?
qa.a: It made Samir realise how far they had drifted, and that Samir was no longer part of her important moments.

qa.q: What changes helped Samir and Disha stay close?
qa.a: Samir apologised, asked real questions instead of sending memes, and they started small shared habits like a weekly playlist.

qa.q: How might Disha have felt when Samir called and apologised?
qa.a: She may have been relieved and happy that Samir still cared, since they talked for two hours.

grounding: A young adult reflects on letting a close friendship drift across distance and taking steps to sustain it.

passage:
Hostel warden's note, final year:
Karthik and Hrithik were roommates for three years and very close. This year Hrithik moved off campus for an internship, and Karthik seemed low; he mentioned that Hrithik was always "too busy" to reply. I suggested he try something small and concrete rather than waiting. He decided to invite Hrithik for Saturday breakfast at the mess, like old times.
Hrithik came, a bit late and tired. They sat together for an hour, and I heard them laughing. Afterwards, Karthik told me Hrithik had been feeling guilty and overwhelmed, not uninterested.
Follow-up: they now have breakfast every other Saturday. Karthik seems more settled.

qa.q: What did Karthik invite Hrithik for?
qa.a: He invited him for Saturday breakfast at the mess.

qa.q: What had Hrithik been feeling, according to Karthik?
qa.a: He had been feeling guilty and overwhelmed, not uninterested in the friendship.

qa.q: Why was the warden's suggestion useful?
qa.a: A small, concrete invitation was easier for a busy friend to accept than waiting for replies, and it led to an honest talk.

qa.q: How might Hrithik see the regular breakfasts?
qa.a: He might feel relieved to have a simple way to stay connected despite his busy internship.

grounding: A warden's note shows young adults sustaining a friendship across new schedules with small regular plans.

passage:
Tuesday, 11:40 pm
Sabina's voice note came at lunch, seven minutes long, about her new lab in Pune and a landlady who hums film songs at 6 am. I listened in two parts between classes and grinned like an idiot. Then I realised I hadn't replied to her last one for nine days. Nine! Not because I don't care. Just placements, assignments, laundry, sleep. Scary how easily a four-year friendship turns into 'haha same' replies. So tonight I sent a real one back, and we fixed a thing: every second Saturday, a call while we both cook dinner, no cancelling unless someone is sick. She said, 'Deal, Karthik, and you have to show me your terrible sambar.' Wrote it in my planner in red. Friendships apparently need calendar slots now. Fine. She's worth a slot.

qa.q: What did Karthik and Sabina agree to do every second Saturday?
qa.a: Have a call while they both cook dinner, with no cancelling unless someone is sick.

qa.q: What worried Karthik on realising there had been no reply for nine days?
qa.a: Karthik was scared their four-year friendship could shrink into shallow 'haha same' replies because of busyness, not lack of care.

qa.q: Why does a fixed slot help a friendship like this?
qa.a: It stops the friendship depending on spare time, which busy weeks rarely have; a regular, easy ritual like cooking together keeps it going.

qa.q: How might Sabina have felt getting Karthik's real reply after nine days?
qa.a: Probably relieved and valued; her teasing about Karthik's sambar suggests she was glad to be back to their easy closeness 😊

grounding: Shows keeping a long friendship alive across cities and busy schedules by setting up a regular shared ritual.

passage:
Rekha: u alive?? last msg from you was 3 weeks ago 😅
Simran: barely. new internship + evening classes. I'm so sorry
Rekha: not a guilt trip. I just miss you
Simran: miss you too. honestly I keep thinking I'll call when I have a free hour and that hour never comes
Rekha: same here tbh. ok what if we stop waiting for the free hour
Rekha: I walk to the metro at 8:10 every morning. you?
Simran: bus at 8:15!
Rekha: 15 min call on the commute, mon and thu?
Simran: yes. even if we just complain about traffic
Rekha: especially then
Simran: also I'm coming to Jaipur in December, keeping one evening only for you
Rekha: writing it in pen 🎉
Simran: ❤️

qa.q: What time does Rekha walk to the metro?
qa.a: At 8:10 every morning.

qa.q: What did Rekha mean when Rekha said 'not a guilt trip'?
qa.a: Rekha wanted Simran to know there was no anger about the silence, only missing Simran and wanting to reconnect.

qa.q: Why is the commute call a good plan?
qa.a: It uses time they already have instead of waiting for a free hour that never comes, and it is short enough to keep up in busy weeks.

qa.q: If Rekha had sent an angry message instead, what might have changed?
qa.a: Simran might have felt more guilty and pulled back further, making it harder to reconnect.

grounding: Shows two friends keeping their connection alive despite distance and busy schedules by fitting calls into their commutes.
